function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
I’ve kept the structure minimal so you can copy‑paste the snippets directly.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone the repo or push changes for you, but the commands below will get you from “clone” to “push” in a few minutes.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine is small & fast
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first (so we can cache npm install)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *If your app listens on a different port, change `EXPOSE 3000` and the `targetPort` in the Kubernetes manifest accordingly.*

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes manifests

Create a folder `k8s/` (or any name you prefer) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry if needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP          # change to NodePort/LoadBalancer if you need external access
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip** – If you want the service to be reachable from outside the cluster, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port`/`targetPort` mapping as needed.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # ---- Node.js setup ----------------------------------------------------
    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'          # match the Docker base image

    # ---- Install dependencies --------------------------------------------
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # ---- Run tests (optional) --------------------------------------------
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    # ---- Build Docker image ------------------------------------------------
    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

    # ---- Log in to GitHub Container Registry -----------------------------
    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    # ---- Push Docker image -------------------------------------------------
    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Why GHCR?**  
> GitHub’s Container Registry (`ghcr.io`) is free for public repos and integrates nicely with GitHub Actions.  
> If you prefer Docker Hub or another registry, replace the `image:` tag in the deployment and the login/push steps accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the `main` branch, building the Docker image and pushing it to GHCR.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the workflow finishes, you can verify the image exists:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>
```

And you can apply the Kubernetes manifests to a cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

That’s it! 🎉

Feel free to tweak the replica count, ports, or registry details to match your environment. If you run into any hiccups, let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
